pages.text: Sharks have existed for more than 450 million years. They were swimming in the world's oceans before trees existed, before dinosaurs, before almost everything that is alive today. They survived the mass extinction that killed the dinosaurs 66 million years ago. They survived three other mass extinctions before that. Of all the animals on earth, sharks have proved the most resilient. They are now seriously threatened. The threat is us.

image.note: Illustration of a great white shark underwater, light filtering from above

pages.text: There are more than 500 species of shark. They range in size from the dwarf lanternshark, which fits in a human hand, to the whale shark, which can reach 12 metres and is the largest fish in the world. Most sharks are between one and three metres long. Most are not dangerous to humans.

Sharks are found in every ocean on earth. They live at the surface and at depths of more than 2,000 metres. Several species can survive in fresh water: bull sharks have been found in rivers far from the sea, including in the Niger River delta. The adaptability of sharks to different environments has been one of the keys to their evolutionary success.

A shark's skin is not smooth. It is covered in microscopic tooth-like scales called dermal denticles, all pointing backward, which cut drag and let the shark slip through water in near silence. The technology is so effective that engineers have copied it for competitive swimsuits and even aircraft surfaces. Stroke a shark from head to tail and it feels like fine sandpaper; stroke it the other way and it can graze skin. The shark wears armour and a speed suit at once.

Sharks are cartilaginous fish: their skeletons are made from cartilage rather than bone. Cartilage is lighter and more flexible than bone, giving sharks their distinctive combination of power and agility. Because cartilage does not fossilise as well as bone, the ancient history of sharks is known mainly from their teeth, which are made of harder material and survive millions of years in sediment.

Shark teeth are extraordinary. A shark produces not one set of teeth but many, growing replacement teeth throughout its lifetime. A great white shark may go through tens of thousands of teeth in its lifetime. Each new tooth is sharper than the last. Shark teeth are replaced continuously, moving forward as older teeth fall out, like a conveyor belt of permanent sharpness.

image.note: Diagram showing shark tooth conveyor belt: multiple rows with arrows indicating forward movement

pages.text: Sharks detect their prey through several sensory systems that work together. Their sense of smell is highly sensitive; they can detect blood in water at a concentration of one part per million. They have a lateral line, a sensory organ running along both sides of the body that detects pressure waves and vibrations in the water. They also have electroreceptors in their snouts, called the ampullae of Lorenzini, that detect the faint electrical fields produced by the muscle contractions of living animals.

The great white shark has an internal system for maintaining body temperature slightly above that of the surrounding water, giving it a performance advantage in cold water that most fish cannot match. It can breach, launching its entire body out of the water when attacking prey from below. The force required to achieve this, applied by an animal of that size and weight, is extraordinary.

Different sharks live utterly different lives. The whale shark, the largest fish on earth, is a gentle giant that filters tiny plankton and lets divers swim alongside it. The tiny cookiecutter shark gouges round plugs of flesh from whales and even, occasionally, submarines. The wobbegong lies flat on the seabed disguised as a carpet of weed. Grouping them all as menacing predators is like grouping every mammal with the wolf. Diversity, not danger, is the shark's real headline.

Some sharks perform one of nature's strangest feats: they navigate the open ocean as if reading a map. Using the earth's magnetic field, smell, and memory, sharks return year after year to precise breeding and feeding grounds thousands of kilometres apart. Great whites tagged off one coast have turned up months later on the far side of an ocean and then come home again. How a fish holds such a map in its head remains one of the sea's great unsolved puzzles.

chapters.title: Sharks of the Gulf of Guinea

pages.text: The Gulf of Guinea, on Nigeria's coast, is home to several shark species. The hammerhead shark, with its distinctive flattened, extended head that places its eyes wide apart, giving it a panoramic field of vision, is found in these waters. The bull shark, one of the species most involved in attacks on humans, is present in the coastal waters and river mouths.

Nigerian fishing communities have historically caught sharks as part of their broader catch. Shark fins have commercial value in Asian markets, where they are used in shark fin soup, a luxury dish. This demand has driven targeted shark fishing, called finning, in which sharks are caught, their fins removed, and the body discarded at sea. The shark, unable to swim without its fins, sinks and drowns. This practice is widely condemned and illegal in many countries, but it continues.

image.note: Illustration comparing a shark with fins intact versus the cruel practice of finning shown abstractly

pages.text: The oceanic whitetip shark was once described by the oceanographer Jacques Cousteau as the most dangerous of all sharks, encountered in open water after shipwrecks and plane crashes. Its populations have declined by more than 95 percent in the past 60 years due to overfishing. A species that was once one of the most abundant large animals in the ocean is now classified as critically endangered.

Sharks matter to West Africa in a very practical way. As top predators, they keep fish populations healthy by removing the sick and the slow, which keeps the whole food web in balance for the fishing communities that depend on it. When sharks are stripped out for the fin trade, the balance tips: prey species boom, then crash, and fisheries suffer. Protecting sharks in the Gulf of Guinea is not sentiment. It is food security for coastal Nigeria.

chapters.title: Why Sharks Matter and Why They Are Threatened

pages.text: Sharks are apex predators or near-apex predators in the ocean food web. Their presence regulates the populations of the animals below them in the food chain. When sharks are removed, those populations expand, which in turn depletes the populations below them, and so on down the food chain. The collapse of a shark population triggers cascading effects throughout the ecosystem.

More than 100 million sharks are killed by humans every year, through targeted fishing, as bycatch in nets set for other species, and through finning. This rate of killing is unsustainable. Sharks reproduce slowly: most species reach sexual maturity late and produce few offspring. They cannot replace their populations at the rate at which they are being killed.

The threat of shark attack, which drives considerable hostility toward sharks in coastal communities, is statistically tiny. In an average year, fewer than ten people are killed by sharks worldwide. In the same year, humans kill more than 100 million sharks. The animal that poses the greater danger in this relationship is not the shark.

image.note: Infographic: sharks killed by humans per year vs humans killed by sharks per year

pages.text: Protecting sharks means protecting the ocean. The ocean's productivity, on which billions of people depend for food, depends on the health of its ecosystems. The health of those ecosystems depends on having apex predators present in sufficient numbers to regulate the food web. This is not sentiment. It is ecology.

The tide may be turning for sharks. Dozens of countries have banned shark finning or created sanctuaries where sharks cannot be fished at all. Divers now pay handsomely to see living sharks, giving coastal communities a reason to protect rather than kill them: a reef shark is worth far more alive, over its life, than dead on a market slab. Four hundred and fifty million years of survival brought sharks this far. Whether they survive us is, for the first time, a question with a human answer.
